sections.title: Mental model — hard = constraints stacked on patterns you own

blocks.md: Every 'Hard' array problem here is a known pattern wearing a constraint costume: in-place-only, no-division, duplicates-heavy, or streaming. The interview game: NAME the base pattern, then solve the constraint explicitly.
**Constraint stated out loud is half-solved. 'In-place ⇒ write-pointer/cyclic tricks. No-division ⇒ prefix-suffix sweeps.'**

items.q: 'Constant space' on array problems usually signals…
items.explain: Reuse the array itself as memory.

sections.title: Trapping Rain Water — two-pointer proof culture

blocks.md: Water over i = min(maxLeft, maxRight) − h[i]. Brute needs both max arrays (O(n) space). Two-pointer version computes on the fly using ONE invariant: **the side with smaller running-max is already decided** — its water can't grow by waiting.

blocks.label: the canonical solution

chain.q: Why is processing the smaller side always safe?
chain.a: If a[l]≤a[r], then right side GUARANTEES a wall ≥ a[l]; true right-max ≥ a[r] ≥ a[l] means min(maxL,maxR) is already pinned by left's running max — nothing later can raise it.
Monotonic decreasing stack pops when taller bar arrives — resolves trapped layers horizontally. Same total, different accounting; expect follow-up to compare.
Boundary min-heap flooding — pointer logic dies in 2D; say so and sketch heap-water-line approach.

blocks.md: **Dictionary order dance: find longest non-increasing SUFFIX → pivot = element before it → swap pivot with smallest-just-larger in suffix → reverse suffix.**

blocks.label: implementation skeleton
blocks.py:
i = n - 2
while i >= 0 and a[i] >= a[i+1]: i -= 1     # find pivot
if i >= 0:
    j = n - 1
    while a[j] <= a[i]: j -= 1              # successor
    a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
a[i+1:] = reversed(a[i+1:])                  # reverse suffix

options: suffix already non-increasing ⇒ reverse = ascending for free
items.explain: Sort would work but waste log factor; reversal exploits structure.

items.title: Trapping Rain Water
items.statement: Three solutions expected: prefix arrays → stack → two-pointer; defend the invariant.

solutionCode.label: two pointers — the smaller side is always decided
solutionCode.py:
def trap(h: list[int]) -> int:
    l, r = 0, len(h) - 1
    left_max = right_max = water = 0
    while l < r:
        if h[l] < h[r]:
            # left is the smaller side, so left_max alone bounds the water here
            left_max = max(left_max, h[l])
            water += left_max - h[l]
            l += 1
        else:
            right_max = max(right_max, h[r])
            water += right_max - h[r]
            r -= 1
    return water

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(1) for the two-pointer form. The prefix-array form is O(n) space; the stack form is O(n) worst case.

followups.q: State the invariant that makes the two-pointer version correct.
followups.a: Water above index i is min(maxLeft(i), maxRight(i)) − h[i]. When h[l] < h[r] you know some bar at or before r is at least h[r] > h[l], so maxRight(l) ≥ h[l]; therefore the min is decided by leftMax and you can commit l without ever seeing the true right maximum. That is the "smaller side is decided" sentence.

followups.q: Walk the three solutions and their trade-offs.
followups.a: Prefix arrays: precompute maxLeft and maxRight, O(n) time and O(n) space — easiest to justify. Monotonic decreasing stack: resolve each basin as a bar pops, O(n)/O(n), natural if you already framed it as "next greater element". Two pointers: O(n)/O(1), fastest and smallest, but needs the invariant above stated explicitly.

items.title: Next Permutation
items.statement: In-place next dictionary order; wrap-around to ascending.

solutionCode.label: find pivot, swap with next-larger suffix element, reverse suffix

items.complexity: Time O(n) — one scan back, one scan for the swap, one reverse. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why is reversing the suffix correct rather than sorting it?
followups.a: The suffix was non-increasing before the swap, and swapping a[i] with the rightmost strictly-greater element preserves that property. A non-increasing sequence reversed is sorted ascending, so reverse achieves the sort in O(n) instead of O(n log n).

followups.q: What happens on a fully descending array like [3,2,1]?
followups.a: The first loop runs off the front with i = −1, so no swap happens and the whole array is reversed to [1,2,3]. That is the required wrap-around to the smallest permutation, handled by the same code path rather than a special case.

items.title: Maximum Product Subarray
items.statement: Track curMax AND curMin; zeros reset; negatives flip roles.
hints: Candidates: x, curMax*x, curMin*x — take best/worst trio.

solutionCode.label: carry both extremes because a negative flips them
solutionCode.py:
def max_product(a: list[int]) -> int:
    cur_max = cur_min = best = a[0]
    for x in a[1:]:
        c1, c2 = cur_max * x, cur_min * x
        cur_max = max(x, c1, c2)   # a negative x makes the old MIN the new MAX
        cur_min = min(x, c1, c2)
        best = max(best, cur_max)
    return best

followups.q: Give the sign-flip sentence before you code.
followups.a: "Multiplying by a negative swaps the roles of my best and worst running products, so a large negative running minimum is one negative away from being the maximum." That is why one running extreme is not enough here, unlike Kadane on sums.

followups.q: How do zeros behave without any special-casing?
followups.a: At a zero all three candidates are 0 or x itself, so including `x` in both max and min effectively restarts the run at that index. The zero cuts the array into independent segments for free.

items.title: Rotate Image (in-place 90°)
items.statement: No extra matrix. Derive mapping aloud, then two-step implement.
hints: Then reverse rows; test odd center untouched.

solutionCode.label: transpose, then reverse each row

items.complexity: Time O(n²) — every cell is touched a constant number of times. Space O(1).

followups.q: Derive why transpose-then-reverse equals a 90° clockwise rotation.
followups.a: A clockwise rotation sends (r,c) to (c, n−1−r). Transpose sends (r,c) to (c,r). Reversing each row then sends (c,r) to (c, n−1−r). Composing the two gives exactly the rotation map.

followups.q: Why must the inner loop start at j = i + 1?
followups.a: Starting at 0 visits each pair twice and swaps it back, leaving the matrix unchanged. Starting at i+1 covers strictly the upper triangle, and the diagonal (i == j) is a fixed point that needs no swap — which is also why an odd-sized matrix leaves its centre untouched.

items.title: Set Matrix Zeroes
items.statement: O(m+n) then O(1) versions — show both, defend flag bookkeeping.
hints: First row/col as notebooks; firstZeroRow/col booleans.
Second pass applies marks skipping marker cells until final step.

solutionCode.label: first row/col as notebooks, plus two scalar flags

items.complexity: Time O(m·n). Space O(1) using the first row and column as the marker store.

followups.q: Why are the two boolean flags necessary at all?
followups.a: Cell m[0][0] is shared by the row-0 notebook and the col-0 notebook, so it cannot record both independently. The flags capture whether row 0 and column 0 were originally zero, before the notebooks overwrite that information.

followups.q: Why must the first row and column be zeroed last?
followups.a: They are the marker store. Zeroing them earlier would flood the notebooks with zeros and cause the interior pass to blank cells that should have survived.

items.title: Spiral Matrix
items.statement: Layered boundary collection; survive 1×n / n×1 torture tests.

solutionCode.label: four shrinking boundaries, re-check between legs

items.complexity: Time O(m·n) — each cell emitted once. Space O(1) beyond the output.

followups.q: Why do the third and fourth legs need guards the first two do not?
followups.a: The first two legs run immediately after the while-condition is checked, so their bounds are known good. By the third leg, `top` and `right` have already moved, so a 1×n or n×1 remainder can make the bottom row identical to the top row — replaying it without the guard duplicates elements.

followups.q: Test it on a single row [[1,2,3]].
followups.a: Leg 1 emits 1,2,3 and top becomes 1. Leg 2’s range is empty. The `top <= bottom` guard is now false, so the bottom leg is skipped rather than re-emitting 3,2,1. Output is [1,2,3], correct.

items.title: Product Except Self — division-free defense
items.statement: Already solved at L2? Now: O(1) extra-output version + explain why division fails on single-zero inputs.
hints: Output array holds left-products; backward sweep folds right-running.
Zero cases: one zero → all-zero except that cell; two+ → all zero.

solutionCode.label: output doubles as the prefix buffer

items.complexity: Time O(n) in two sweeps. Space O(1) auxiliary — the output array is the scratch space.

followups.a: With no zeros, total/a[i] works. With exactly one zero, every position except the zero must be 0, and the zero position must hold the product of the rest — total/a[i] is a division by zero there. With two or more zeros every output is 0. So division needs a zero count and three branches, while the two-sweep version needs none.

followups.q: Where does the O(1) claim actually come from?
followups.a: The output array is required by the problem, so it is excluded from the auxiliary budget by convention. What matters is that the right-hand products are carried in a single scalar rather than a second length-n array — that is the improvement over the naive prefix/suffix pair.
